newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada will lead G7 growth in '97 and '98 - bank.
newsitem.headline: Canada will lead G7 growth in '97 and '98 - bank.

text.p: Canada will have the fastest growing economy of any Group of Seven nation for the next two years, powered by interest rates at 40-year lows, Toronto-Dominion Bank predicted on Tuesday.

Canada's fifth largest bank forecast the economy will growth by 3.5 percent in 1997 and 3.2 percent in 1998. Consumers are expected to lead the growth as low interest rates and rising employment encourage people to spend.
"The Canadian consumer is back," T-D chief economist Ruth Getter said in a statement. "We are now reaping the full rewards of low interest rates."
The bank said it expected about 300,000 jobs to be created this year and next, up from 180,000 jobs last year.

But the unemployment rate was expected to come down only gradually, as better prospects lured discourage workers back into the labor force. TD predicted an unemployment rate of 9.4 percent in 1997, 9 percent in 1998 and 8.6 percent in 1999.
Canadian short-term interest rates were "likely to rise slightly" in early 1998, but should remain below U.S. rates for the foreseeable future, the bank said.
TD also expected the Canadian dollar to rise gradually, reaching US$0.736 (C$1.3587) in 1998 and almost US$0.75 (C$1.33) by 1999.
Among Canadian provinces, oil-rich Alberta was expected to have the strongest economy this year, with a growth rate of 4.4 percent.

Newfoundland -- a have-not province -- was expected to lead growth among the provinces in the next two years. Newfoundland's economy was expected to grow by 4.9 percent in 1998 and 5.2 percent in 1999 as the Hibernia offshore oil and Voisey's Bay mining projects got under way.
Overall, the Canadian economy was benefiting from smaller goverment deficits, a current account surplus and a low inflation rate, TD economists said.

"The outlook for the Canadian economy is the best it has been this decade," said Getter. "We have gone through a long period of retrenchment and adjustment, and we are now able to enjoy the benefits."
